Day of Judgment
DAY uv JUJ-ment
n. phrase (eschatological; the appointed day on which God will judge all persons, living and dead, through Jesus Christ, rendering eternal verdicts of life or condemnation)
Day from Old English dæg (period of time, the daytime, a fixed day). Judgment from Latin judicamentum, from judicare (to judge, decide), from jus (law, right) + dicare (to say, proclaim). The phrase names the eschatological appointed day — singular, fixed, and already determined by God (Acts 17:31) — on which the risen Christ will preside over the comprehensive and final adjudication of every human life, every secret word, and every hidden deed.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Day of Judgment is the eschatological moment appointed by God at which the risen and exalted Christ will judge all persons who have ever lived — both the righteous and the wicked — rendering final, irreversible verdicts of eternal life or eternal condemnation. Acts 17:31 provides the apostolic summary: God “has fixed a day in which He will judge the world in righteousness — through a Man whom He has appointed, having furnished proof to all men by raising Him from the dead.” The Resurrection of Christ is the public certification of His appointment as Judge; the fixed day is already set. Revelation 20:11–15 provides the most detailed prophetic vision: the Great White Throne, the resurrection of all the dead, the opening of the books, and the judgment according to deeds, with the Book of Life determining the final verdict. Matthew 12:36 extends the scope to every dimension of human life: “every careless word that men shall speak — they shall render account for it in the day of judgment.” Second Corinthians 5:10 addresses the church directly: “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” — the believer's judgment is not for condemnation (Rom 8:1) but for accounting of stewardship. The 1689 LBCF (Chapter 32) and Westminster Confession (Chapter 33) both affirm a final judgment of all persons, body and soul, with eternal life for the elect and eternal punishment for the reprobate — in accordance with the works done in the body as evidence of, not the ground of, saving faith.

Webster 1828 Definition

The appointed, fixed eschatological day on which Christ will judge all persons, living and dead — the wicked to condemnation, the righteous to eternal life — with final, irreversible verdicts rendered in accordance with every word and deed; grounded in Acts 17:31 and Revelation 20:11–15.

DAY OF JUDGMENT, n. phrase. The singular, divinely appointed eschatological event at which the risen Jesus Christ will exercise the function of universal Judge over all persons — every human being who has ever lived, whether previously living or deceased — rendering final, irreversible verdicts of eternal life or eternal condemnation. Acts 17:31 calls it a “fixed day” set in the eternal counsel of God, the certainty of which is attested by Christ's bodily resurrection.

Revelation 20:11–15 is the most vivid prophetic description: a great white throne, a Judge before whom “earth and heaven fled away,” the resurrection of all the dead (small and great alike), the opening of the books of human deeds, and the Book of Life as the determinative register. Those not found in the Book of Life are cast into the lake of fire — the second death. The judgment is according to deeds (v. 13) as the evidence of what each person was, not as the meritorious ground of their standing.

Matthew 12:36 expands the scope: “every careless word that men shall speak — they shall render account for it in the day of judgment.” No dimension of human life falls outside the scope of the final accounting — not merely the great moral choices but the idle word, the secret motivation, the private thought. Ecclesiastes 12:14 makes the same point: “God will bring every act to judgment, everything which is hidden, whether it is good or evil.”

For the believer, 2 Corinthians 5:10 (“we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ”) is not a threat of condemnation — Romans 8:1 settles that: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” The believer's judgment at the Bema seat of Christ (2 Cor 5:10; Rom 14:10) is the judgment of a servant before a master — a rendering of account for stewardship, with rewards and losses, but not with eternal condemnation. The wicked face a different tribunal: the Great White Throne (Rev 20:11) where the verdict is condemnation.

The 1689 LBCF (Chapter 32–33) and Westminster Confession (Chapter 33) both affirm a general resurrection of all persons and a final judgment with two eternal outcomes: the elect to everlasting life and the reprobate to everlasting punishment. The confession's purpose in the doctrine is pastoral: the believer should find comfort in knowing that all injustice will be addressed; the unbeliever should find its weight a summons to flee to Christ now.

Key Scripture

Revelation 20:12 — "And I saw the dead, the great and the small, standing before the throne. And books were opened — and another book was opened, which is the Book of Life. And the dead were judged from the things written in the books, according to their deeds."

Acts 17:31 — "Because He has fixed a day in which He will judge the world in righteousness — through a Man whom He has appointed, having furnished proof to all men by raising Him from the dead."

Matthew 12:36 — "And I say to you, that every careless word that men shall speak — they shall render account for it in the day of judgment."

2 Corinthians 5:10 — "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ — so that each one may be recompensed for his deeds in the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad."

Modern Corruption

Universalism denies the Day of Judgment's condemnatory outcome by asserting all will eventually be saved; annihilationism denies its eternality by holding the wicked will be extinguished; and therapeutic Christianity effectively postpones it indefinitely by suppressing preaching on hell and final accountability.

expand to see more

Universalism — in both its classical (Origen, Gregory of Nyssa) and modern forms (Thomas Talbott, Robin Parry's The Evangelical Universalist, Rob Bell's Love Wins) — holds that the love of God will ultimately prevail over every human will, producing the final salvation of all persons (and, in some versions, even fallen angels). On this account, the Day of Judgment has no permanent condemning outcome; it is at most a temporal purging preparatory to universal reconciliation. This position is incompatible with Revelation 20:10 (“they will be tormented day and night forever and ever”), Matthew 25:46 (“these will go away into eternal punishment”), and 2 Thessalonians 1:9 (“eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord”). The Westminster Confession and 1689 LBCF explicitly affirm the wicked's “everlasting misery.”

Annihilationism — the view that the wicked are extinguished at judgment rather than enduring conscious eternal punishment — has been defended by John Stott, Clark Pinnock, and Edward Fudge, often on the grounds of divine justice (endless punishment for finite sin is disproportionate) and the meaning of olethros (destruction). Evangelical conditionalists cite Revelation 20:14 (“the second death”) as pointing to cessation. The Reformed confessional response is that “second death” is glossed within Revelation itself as the lake of fire, and that the language of “torment day and night forever and ever” (Rev 20:10) for the devil and the beast requires a conscious subject to be tormented. Minimizing the weight of the judgment removes from the church its most urgent evangelistic motive: the Day of Judgment is a fixed appointment that no one can avoid, and the gospel is the only route to a verdict of acquittal.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Day of Judgment is rooted in the Old Testament Day of the LORD tradition, the Synoptic judgment teachings of Jesus, Paul's Areopagus address, the Revelation 20 vision, and the Reformed confessional doctrine of the last things.

expand to see more

Day of the LORD (Amos 5:18–20; Joel 2; Zeph 1) — the Old Testament prophetic precursor; the Day of the LORD is a day of darkness and reckoning, not of automatic blessing; the New Testament Day of Judgment is its ultimate eschatological fulfillment.

Matthew 25:31–46 — the parable of the sheep and the goats; the Son of Man as universal Judge separating all nations; the two destinies — eternal life and eternal punishment — stated with the same adverb (aionios, “eternal”) for both outcomes.

Acts 17:30–31 — Paul's Areopagus proclamation; the Day of Judgment as the public rationale for the universal call to repentance; the Resurrection as God's proof of Christ's appointment as Judge.

Revelation 20:11–15 — the Great White Throne judgment; the most detailed prophetic vision of the final judgment in Scripture; the Book of Life as the determinative register and the second death as the final verdict for the condemned.

1689 LBCF, Chapters 32–33 / Westminster Confession, Chapter 33 — the confessional Reformed doctrine of the resurrection and final judgment; the two eternal outcomes stated explicitly; the Day of Judgment as the moment at which God's moral governance of history reaches its public vindication.

Usage

"The doctrine of the Day of Judgment should drive evangelism: Acts 17:30–31 reveals that it is precisely because God has fixed a judgment day that He now commands all people everywhere to repent; the urgency of mission is eschatological."

"The believer's judgment at the Bema seat (2 Cor 5:10) is distinct from the Great White Throne judgment (Rev 20:11) — the believer stands before Christ not to receive a verdict on eternal destiny (which is settled in justification) but to render an account of stewardship, with rewards and losses but no condemnation."

"Matthew 12:36 (“every careless word”) is a word of weight for preachers: the same standard that convicts the impenitent will reveal whether every sermon, every counsel, and every word of comfort was faithful — the Day of Judgment is not only a fact to proclaim but a motive for faithfulness in one's own ministry."
